Ancient Knowledge is a strategic card game in which you erect monuments and build artefacts to pass on your knowledge. Time will make your constructions ephemeral,so make the right decision and combine the many cards at your disposal, because all knowledge is doomed to disappear… It's up to you to find the best synergy so that you can pass down knowledge before the decline of the emblematic monuments you have constructed, monuments we still find nowadays in the four corners of the globe. From Mexican pyramids to the Sphinx of Giza, passing through the famous cities of Tiwanaku and Babylon, only the cleverest builder will shine through the ages and seize victory. In this game, your only enemy is time. Prove to your opponents that you are the worthly representative of your Legacy! Will your monuments withstand the trial of time? Place it in the numbered space indicated by the circle. Place a number of knowledge tokens on it equal to the Knowledge symbol. If it has an instant effect, apply as much as possible. A monument can be played in a space other than where it wishes as long as it does not contain the lock symbol, and you discard extra cards equal to the difference between where it wants to be and where you want to put it e.g. if it's a 4 and you want it in space 6, discard an extra 2 cards. For each numbered area, place your first monument on the lower space, and your second monument on the upper space, you cannot have a third monument for each numbered space. If you have two monuments in a numbered space, and the lower monument is removed due to some effect, slide the upper monument down so it becomes the new lower monument. Any effects which mention adjacency only affect orthogonal adjacency. If you play an Artifact, play it in one of your 5 starting artifact spaces on your player board. Once all 5 spaces are taken, you cannot play more artifacts until some effect gives you an empty space again. [Rating: 1/10] If you dont get the right cards, you nealry cant do anything. Its fully based on luck, worst game i ever played. If an opponent gets early the right artifacts becomes unbeatable.

[Rating: 2/10] The textbook definition of multi-player solitaire and the exact type of gameplay that I despise in a game. Won't ever play or recommend unless MPS is your thing.

[Rating: 2/10] After 2 play sessions, live and on BGA, I would rate it 4/10 – an intriguing mechanical premise with delayed card sequencing, but it lacks strategic depth and fails to evolve into a cohesive and substantively engaging game.  +2 more plays and you have seen it all. The game is really just about the "knowledge" management, thus completely uninteresting. (2/10) Copy sold!

[Rating: 3/10] Multiplayer solitaire except for a common tableau of cards and shitty take that effects. I just hate this kind of design. It's such a shame, because otherwise it has some neat stuff in it, although even the cards moving is underwhelming.

[Rating: 3/10] I had high hopes for this game but they were all swiftly dashed. While the key mechanism of placing out monuments and using the order and manner in which they decline initially seemed interesting, in reality it soon proved annoyingly fiddly and actually rather dull. There is also a frankly ludicrous disparity in utility between a great many of the cards which leaves the game prone to being massively impacted by sheer luck. Apparently Race for the Galaxy was a big inspiration for this but this is a far inferior product which lacks the snappiness, genuine scope for clever play and more engaging 

[Rating: 3/10] Overhype anyone? The maiden voyage was a disaster and I'm not sure I want to bother with another try. This is an AP trap made worse with wildly varying turn lengths based on what actions you are performing. I also didn't see anything that distinguishes it from the flood of games that have 1000 unique cards that force you to read the whole game rather than interacting with people. There is an activity called reading that is better than board games if I want to do that. Reading a book also takes less time than slogging through this.

[Rating: 3/10] My initial play of this was pretty good (base game), incorporating the expansion however, I ran into a problem that completely obliterated my desire to play it: the deck is too fucking big, and the comobo's are mostly an afterthought. The central idea of a depleting tableau is interesting, but the problem is that it's so focused on this aspect that all other considerations for gameplay are basically tossed aside. This would be totally fine, if you didn't have to mill the deck constantly to get a reasonable hand of cards, which seem to otherwise end up as disparate and completely non cohesive. 

[Rating: 3/10] Tableau builder where your cards get conveyored into history. The ancient architecture theme is a potentially rich one, but it's wasted and narratively opaque in practice, with the token/card-moving engines you build feeling almost completely abstract. They're not very interesting mechanically either.

[Rating: 3/10] Engine building game, but flawed engine. If you start with bad cards and the others get good cards you can never come back. I was picking my nose for 70 minutes while my friends enjoyed the streamlined engine.

[Rating: 3/10] Boring interactions, you have nothing to do in other players turn and it  makes long, boring waiting time between your turns. As an engine builder, it lacks choices and does not provide good feeling that you actually improving anything. You cant follow other players victory points, you have absolutely no idea who is leading. No theme. Overall it is not a good game. 3/10

[Rating: 3/10] A bad game. From absolutely no theme to having to read every single card, nothing is exciting. This would be a nightmare playing with 4, or even with 3. Turns can take forever, since you have 2 actions: imagine drawing 10 cards with your first action, reading through them all, checking the open market for possible synergies, all the while no one else has absolutely nothing to do while you crunch the numbers.
